client: Ever since my grandma passed away last month, I’ve been struggling to focus on my university work. I keep feeling this heavy sadness that makes it hard to even start my assignments, and I’m not sure if talking about it here will really help me move forward.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of grief that's making everyday tasks feel overwhelming right now. While your words show sadness, I notice a slight hesitation in your voice that makes me wonder if you're also feeling uncertain about whether things can improve. Would it help to explore how this loss has specifically affected your ability to focus on schoolwork?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, schoolwork has been really hard since my mom passed. I sit down to study and just end up staring at the page, thinking about how she'll never see me graduate. Part of me wants to push through for her, but another part thinks what's the point if she's not here to see it? 

I don't know if talking about it will help - it's not like it'll bring her back. The grief just feels too big sometimes.
therapist: I hear both the deep love for your mom and the painful conflict in your voice - wanting to honor her while struggling with the unfairness of her absence. The way your thoughts jump between memories, future milestones, and doubts tells me this grief is still very raw and overwhelming right now. Would it help to talk about what your mom might say about continuing your education, if she were here with you today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if imagining what she'd say helps...it just makes me miss her more. Sometimes I think she'd be proud of me for continuing school, but other times I feel guilty for moving forward when she's not here to see it. It's like no matter what I imagine, it just reminds me she's gone.
therapist: I notice your voice tightens when you talk about feeling guilty - it seems there's real pain in this struggle between wanting to make her proud and feeling like you're leaving her behind. That tension between honoring her memory and moving forward must be exhausting to hold alone. Would it help to explore smaller, more manageable ways to remember her that don't feel so overwhelming?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I guess the smaller ways thing makes sense, but part of me feels guilty even considering that. Like if I don't keep punishing myself with the big gestures, I'm letting her down somehow. It's exhausting though, you're right about that—I'm tired of constantly feeling like I'm failing her memory. 

The idea of doing less almost makes me more anxious, like what if she'd think I cared less? I know that probably sounds irrational, but the fear is really strong.
therapist: I hear the exhaustion in your voice as you describe this constant pressure to prove your love through grand gestures. While your words show thoughtful concern about honoring your mom, there's also a quieter sense of weariness that suggests this approach might be taking a heavy toll on you. Could we explore together what your mom truly valued about your relationship, rather than what you feel you need to prove through suffering?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I know she always said the little everyday things mattered most to her—like when I'd call just to chat or bring her favorite tea. But now that she's gone, it feels like those small things weren't enough. If they were, why do I keep having this crushing guilt that I should have done more? 

I get what you're saying about focusing on what she actually valued, but my brain keeps countering with "But what if she was just being nice? What if she really wanted those big displays of love and was too kind to say so?" The doubt eats at me.
therapist:
It's interesting how your voice softens a bit when recalling those sweet everyday moments, even while your words carry such heavy doubt. That tells me part of you still connects with the truth of those simpler expressions of love, even as your anxious thoughts try to convince you otherwise. 

The speed and pitch of your voice suggest this guilt is really racing through your mind—would it help to slow down and examine whether these doubts about "what if she was just being nice" are based in evidence, or in this raw grief that makes everything feel uncertain right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess you're right that part of me still believes those moments were real. But the louder part keeps saying maybe I'm just desperate to believe that, you know? When I try to slow down and look at the evidence, my brain just floods with all the times I messed up or failed to show up for her. It's like the good memories slip right through my fingers.
therapist:
I notice your voice gets quieter and more fragile when you talk about the good memories slipping away - it seems there's real pain in how quickly those positive moments get overshadowed by self-criticism. The way you describe this mental flood suggests your grief might be distorting your ability to hold both the imperfections and the genuine love that existed between you. 

Would it help if we looked at one specific memory where you showed up for her, to counterbalance this overwhelming focus on perceived failures?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... every time I try to think of a good memory, it feels like my brain automatically points out all the ways I could have done better in that moment too. Like even when I did something nice for her, I remember how impatient I got afterward or how I didn't follow through enough. It's like the guilt won't let me have those memories cleanly. 

Maybe if you pick the memory for me? I'm worried I'll just ruin it with criticism again like I always do.
therapist:
I hear both the exhaustion in your voice and the way your thoughts keep circling back to self-criticism - it sounds like you're stuck in a painful pattern where no memory feels safe from this harsh judgment. The quick pace and higher pitch in your voice suggest this is really distressing you in the moment. 

Since you're open to it, let's try this together: remember when you'd bring her favorite tea - can we just stay with that simple image for a moment? Notice how her face looked when you handed it to her, without letting the "buts" and "should haves" interrupt just yet.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I can picture her face when I brought the tea—she'd smile in this soft way that made her eyes crinkle. But then I immediately think about how I should have done that more often, how I took those little moments for granted. It's like even the good memories just turn into more reasons to beat myself up.
therapist: I noticed your voice softened and slowed when describing her crinkling smile - that tells me there's still a tender warmth connected to that memory, even though your thoughts quickly turn to self-criticism. It's understandable to feel regret, but I wonder if we could pause for a moment to honor that sweetness in her reaction, without letting the "should haves" take over just yet?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, I guess there was something nice about that moment. But it just makes me feel worse now, knowing I messed it up. Why does remembering the good stuff have to hurt so much? It's like salt in the wound. 

I don't know how to just focus on the positive without all the regret flooding in. It feels... forced or fake to try to ignore the bad parts.
therapist:
I hear both the tenderness in your voice when recalling that moment and the pain that comes with it now - it's like your grief is pulling you in two directions at once. Your words show you're trying to honor the good while being honest about the regret, and that tension feels very real in your voice. 

Rather than forcing positivity or ignoring the regrets, would it help to acknowledge both feelings as valid parts of your grieving process? They don't have to cancel each other out.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that makes sense, but it's so hard to hold both those feelings at once. When I remember the good times, I feel guilty for not appreciating them enough back then. And when I think about my regrets, it makes the happy memories hurt even more. It's like no matter which way I turn, I end up in pain.
therapist:
I hear how your voice quiets and slows when describing this painful back-and-forth - it sounds like you're carrying both the weight of your love and your regrets simultaneously, and that's understandably exhausting. The way you describe being pulled between these feelings suggests grief isn't moving in straight lines for you right now, but in painful circles. 

Would it help to acknowledge that this very struggle - wishing you'd appreciated her more - is actually proof of how deeply you did love her? The pain exists because the love was real.
